title: Deliver Ripple: the Z-set incremental engine, views, subscriptions, and maintainers (B4)
description:
## What & scope
Deliver `fgdb-ripple`, the Ripple incremental-computation plane (Bet B4): one checked Z-set delta algebra advanced by total committed time powering four features vendors build separately — (1) the registered recursive-query subset, (2) materialized table/graph views, (3) standing queries/changefeeds with the full durable subscription-cursor machine, and (4) eligible incremental analytics maintainers. Child anchors: `w6-zset-circuits` (exact integer Z-sets, annotation families, circuit runtime), `w6-delta-consumption` (canonical `LogicalDeltaBatch`/frontier consumption, expiry/valid-time delta laws, coalesced provenance), `w6-recursion` (incremental fixpoints), `w6-views` (`DerivedGeneration`, `ViewReadPolicy`, constructed-graph identity), `w6-subscriptions` plus subtasks `w6-sub-delivery` and `w6-sub-resets` (the complete §9.5 cursor state machine: baseline/delta/reset unions, leases, capabilities, pause/close/expire), `w6-freshness` (WITH FRESHNESS slo-typed bounds and `FreshnessBreach` notices), `w6-maintainers` (delta-PageRank, incremental connectivity/triangles/k-core, degree/label statistics with staleness contracts), and `w6-triggers` (§9.5's post-commit trigger contract: exactly-once durable scheduling records; external effects at-least-once with a stable idempotency key unless the sink is transactional).

## Why (bets, market, goals)
B4 is one of the six composition bets: "One checked Z-set delta algebra powers the registered recursive-query subset, materialized views, standing queries/subscriptions, and eligible incremental analytics; final committed effects produce the canonical ordered delta batches." The 2026 market synthesis flags derived-state freshness and incremental reindexing as unsolved problems of shipping systems; GraphRAG/agent-memory workloads (B6) need fresh views and change subscriptions over branch-isolated agent state. SOTA verdicts (§3.3): **adopt** DBSP's linear-time core over canonical post-commit deltas — only the validated operator/recursion subset is incremental, and deletion may require retained support state and is not promised equal physical cost; **adapt** incremental analytics as per-algorithm maintainers with recompute fallback and staleness contracts; the vector/FTS ingestion pipelines (§10) are Ripple consumers too, closing the freshness loop for Beacon. B1 supplies the source: committed effects produce the canonical ordered delta batches, so Ripple is a corollary of durability, not a bolted-on streaming system. B5: only registered derivatives are incremental ("for free" is not an operator law), derivative=batch is invariant FG-INV-15, and every statistical claim is typed evidence, never enforcement.

## Design — normative detail
Unification claim (§9.1): recursive evaluation, materialized views, subscriptions, and incremental analytics share computation over Z-sets advanced by a total committed time; the source is never the unresolved intent log but the finalized `LogicalDeltaTemplate` whose canonically sorted coordinate entries are exactly equal to the canonical before/after change, materialized at apply into role-tagged self-contained `LogicalDeltaBatch<LocalCommitted>` / `LogicalDeltaBatch<ShardFragment>` (internal only, never a public CDC source) / `GlobalLogicalDeltaBatch` (the only public W12 source). Every circuit integrates all relevant coordinate entries of a batch or none and records the role-tagged batch ID/idempotency key. Engine (§9.2): exact integer `ZWeight` (checked `i128` promoting before overflow to an in-house canonical signed-limb integer), lift/differentiate/integrate/delay, registered derivatives per GLA operator under Appendix C's incrementalization contracts, factorized delta forms with proved flattening equivalence, spillable LSM-backed arrangements (§8.7). Batch and incremental plans share the typed algebra but carry distinct physical optimization/resource contracts. Runtime placement: Ripple runs in §16's `RippleRegion` bulkhead (view circuits · subscription fan-out · stats maintainers · index feeders), so derived-state lag never destabilizes the transaction path. Delivery of any protected output rides §12.8's audit-visibility pipeline (release) and batched Protocol-plane activation with batch-shaped time evidence (leases); Ripple may never bypass either, which is exactly why freshness statements are slo-class.

## Invariants & claim types
FG-INV-15 binds the whole epic: "For every registered exact derivative, integrating ordered deltas equals batch evaluation, and retained Local/Global batches own each payload exactly once … Every result-producing feature uses one generated, noninterchangeable owner arm and the state-shaped independent-retention machine … Cursor baseline/delta rules forbid delta before baseline ACK and expose every gap. Public digests cover exact authorized canonical bytes/provenance, never keyed object IDs." FG-INV-16: no cursor/output lease is lost, duplicated, refunded, released, or exposed while obligated; audit candidates remain hidden until their exact batch and gap-free visibility advance. Delivery freshness is FG-EVID-04 (slo-class, never an invariant); view/index staleness SLO feasibility is FG-CFG-03; maintenance-stream capacity is FG-CFG-04. §17 benchmark rows (benchmark class): delta application ≥ 1M input-changes/s per circuit worker; subscription end-to-end p99 < 10 ms. §15.5 formal anchor: Ripple proofs cover only the explicitly registered operator/annotation subset.

## Interactions
Consumes `w2-delta-batches` (template/batch/index/frontier stream) and `w2-retention-checkpoints` (GAP/new-baseline transitions at cuts). Operator laws come from `w5-gla-algebra`/`w5-factorization`; views register as rewrite targets for `w5-planner`; `w5-branch-stats` delta layers ride `w6-maintainers`. Beacon (`w7-index-core`, `w7-vector`, `w7-fts`, `w7-path-temporal`) index feeders and dense projections are Ripple consumers; `w8-projection` supplies the recompute fallback. Delivery interlocks with `w9-audit-release` (`AuditVisibilityAdvanceSpec`) and `w9-activation-batching` (`ProtectedOutputActivationBatchSpec`/`ProtectedOutputDispositionBatchSpec`, `TimeBoundSubject::ActivationBatch`); `w10-fgp-core`/`w10-capabilities`/`w10-cdc` frame the public surface; `w12-decision-visibility` publishes the Global batches the Meta frontier consumes.

## Success Criteria
Epic closes when all child anchors close and the G2 slice holds end-to-end: conditional source templates plus self-contained retained Ripple batches; publicly authenticated baseline results and atomic/coalesced delta provenance/output; durable cursor-generation plus tagged baseline/delta lease with baseline-ACK/delta-ACK/resume/lost-response/expiry recovery and no delta-before-baseline or silent gap; table/graph views with explicit read policies. E2E script: commit → template finalization → batch apply → view update → subscription publish → audit release → batched activation → delivery → ACK, with structured logs at every transition (batch IDs, frontiers, pipeline orders, lease IDs, public digests) and crash/restart injection at every arrow. Bench gates as above registered with pinned fixtures/manifests; they execute under §15.6's deterministic apparatus once `verif-perf-apparatus` and the perf-bench suite land — manifests-green is a gate-g4 requirement, not an epic-close-time run.

## Risks & rejected alternatives
Deletion cost: retractions may need retained support state; equal physical cost is never promised. Rejected: Boolean/tropical weights as the change domain (erases the additive inverses needed for deletion); subscriptions as transport-layer tailing of the commit log (leaks internal frontiers/provenance, defeats audit gating); wall-clock freshness bounds (drag time-authority observations onto the fan-out path). Weaver-style refinable timestamps rejected for 1.0 — one global scalar commit order keeps Chronicle, branches, Ripple, and replay simple (§3.4); W12 preserves the contract through the Meta-published Global frontier.

## Provenance
§9 (736–811); §0 B4; §2.4; §3.3; §12.8; §16; §17; §19 W6/G2; Appendix F FG-INV-15/16, FG-EVID-04, FG-CFG-03/04.

title: Epic: Beacon index fabric — snapshot-pinned, authority-correct derived indexes (§10)
description:
## What & scope
W7 delivers Beacon, FrankenGraphDB's index fabric: crates `fgdb-index-core`, `fgdb-btree`, `fgdb-fts`, `fgdb-vector`, and `fgdb-pathidx` (§18.1). Beacon owns every secondary access path: property B-tree/hash indexes, A+-style adjacency views and dense projections, the segment-based full-text index, vector ANN with historical topology, adaptive path/reachability (2-hop/pruned-landmark) indexes, the persistent-union-find temporal-connectivity index, and the hybrid retrieval operator. All kinds implement one shared law set in `fgdb-index-core`: pinned `IndexSnapshot` generations, coverage/ancestry/tail proofs, watermarks in commit-sequence units, and the `IndexAuthority` split. Spatial (`Point`) indexing is explicitly OUT of scope in 1.0 — a registered non-goal owned by g0-format-arms (Z/Hilbert-curve-over-B-tree recorded as the post-1.0 route).

## Why (bets, market, goals)
B1 One Version Universe: an index generation that answers for the wrong branch head, snapshot, or valid-time coordinate is a correctness bug, not a staleness quirk — so every generation pins exact coordinates and selection is a proof-carrying decision. B4 Ripple incrementality: index ingestion pipelines are Ripple consumers (§9.6), so commit→searchable is a structural, measured pipeline. The 2026 market synthesis (§3.3) names the buyer gaps this epic attacks: governance/access control, derived-state freshness, and incremental reindexing — hybrid convergence (text+vector+graph) is where GraphRAG/agent-memory adoption is heading, and §10.4's fresh transactional ANN plus Warden-grade authority is the deliberate leapfrog. B5: recall, staleness, and probe-latency claims are typed (`statistical`/`slo`/`benchmark`), never smuggled in as invariants. B6: agents consume honest `AnswerContract`s and freshness bounds instead of guessing index lag. B2: adjacency views reuse Strata run machinery wholesale rather than inventing a parallel store.

## Design — normative detail
Universal law (§10): every index generation exposes `IndexSnapshot { identity: DerivedIdentity, root_oid, answer_contract: AnswerContract }`; a definition normally has one canonical advancing source role; a query separately supplies target `CoordinateSchemaBinding[]`. A root is direct only at exact binding/frontier equality; it may tail only when each advancing `DerivedSourceCoverage.base_binding.selected_head` is a proved ancestor on that exact branch and a contiguous delta path reaches every target under the shared frontier. A newer/nonancestor root is unusable except through a retained matching historical generation or a separately proved inverse/recompute path. Definition/topology/authority/profile mismatch is never "close enough"; no path silently omits a tail; authorization applies during statistics, candidates, traversal, scoring, and result construction — never as a final filter. `IndexAuthority = ConstraintCriticalSynchronous | DerivedRebuildable`: constraint-critical maps are branch/head/schema-scoped canonical state owned by Chronicle/Txn's `fgdb-constraints` (Beacon supplies access implementation, never asynchronous ownership or a second truth); derived indexes may be discarded. `IndexDefinition` is canonical versioned structure, not opaque DDL; every membership/score/order/recall-population/stopping-affecting parameter is semantic and lives in `definition_oid`/`DerivedIdentity`/`ApproximationProfile`/realized `AnswerContract`; a rebuilt ANN topology is a new semantic generation even from the same DDL. The seven §10 kinds are split across the child beads listed below.

## Invariants & claim types
FG-INV-12: approximate candidate/topology changes create a new pinned semantic generation; no build progress or physical index artifact changes schema visibility before its ordinary transactional SchemaOp activation; every claimed answer-equivalent exact rebuild preserves logical values, multiplicity, order, visibility, security projection, and AnswerContract. FG-INV-18: index/build controls remain invisible until a transactional SchemaOp activates a validated generation; rebuildable indexes/views/caches can be discarded without changing exact answers or authorization. FG-INV-20: authorization precedes every observation or effect across storage, statistics, routing/scoring, temporal selection, and derived state. Claim classes: ANN recall/drift is FG-CAL-03 (`evidence.toml`); index staleness SLO feasibility is FG-CFG-03 (`slo.toml`); derived-state freshness is FG-EVID-04 (slo-class, never an invariant); §17 gates (vector ≥20k QPS at recall ≥0.95; temporal probe <100µs; commit→searchable p50/p99) are `benchmark` class.

## Interactions
Children: w7-index-core (shared kernel), w7-btree, w7-adjacency-views, w7-fts, w7-vector, w7-path-temporal, w7-hybrid. Upstream anchors: w4-index-lifecycle (shadow-build/validate/transactional-activate), w6-delta-consumption (canonical tail stream), w3-seal-compact (segment lifecycle + digest validators), w5-planner and w5-answer-contracts (selection and contracts), w9-enforcement (§12.4 authority reuse law), w4-constraints (constraint-critical ownership). Downstream: w8-kernels consumes dense projections; w10 surfaces expose hybrid search; verif-oracles and perf-freshness-vector verify and gate.

## Success Criteria
Epic closes when every child bead passes the §7.5 per-kind gate battery — differential, metamorphic, crash, stale-tail, definition-drift, policy/revocation, branch-fork/merge, delete, approximation-generation, and rebuild-switch tests — and the §17 rows (vector QPS/recall, temporal probe latency, derived-state freshness p50/p99 with watermark lag) are wired as bench gates with committed baselines, variance budgets, and flamegraph-on-regression — the gate rows, fixtures, and baselines are registered here; the gated runs execute on §15.6's deterministic apparatus once `verif-perf-apparatus`/`perf-freshness-vector` land, with manifests-green a gate-g4 requirement. Additionally required before close: (a) an epic-level e2e script that, over one branched, valid-time-sliced fixture graph, creates one index of every §10 kind, drives sustained commits through the Ripple delta tail, and issues queries at exact-binding, tail-compensated, and reject coordinates for each kind — asserting typed rejection (never silent staleness) on the reject cases; and (b) a detailed-logging conformance bar: every child's implementation and tests must emit structured selection decision records (identity fields compared, tail interval, proof kind, rejection reason), per-delivery watermark-lag samples, and per-generation build/activation/discard lifecycle events, so post-implementation verification can reconstruct every selection and freshness claim from logs alone.

## Risks & rejected alternatives
HNSW under MVCC/capabilities/compaction is a named §20 risk ("known-hard industry-wide"); mitigation is pinned historical authorized roots, complete delta-tail compensation, exact fallback, population-labeled recall evidence — output filtering and exact rerank cannot repair missed candidates. Rejected across the epic: asynchronous constraint indexes (second truth), output filtering as an authority or completeness mechanism, universal polylog temporal-connectivity claims, spatial indexing in 1.0, learned indexes as authoritative access paths (§3.4 rejection (j): a learned structure is never an authoritative access path), and any "close enough" generation reuse.

## Provenance
§10 (814-831), §3.3, §3.4 (rejection (j)), §3.5, §12.4, §17, §18.1, §20, Appendix F.

title: Prism analytics bridge: authorized fnx projections, kernels, witnesses, bulkhead
description:
## What & scope
Deliver Prism, FrankenGraphDB's in-database analytics plane (the `fgdb-prism` crate), exposing franken_networkx (fnx) algorithms as first-class database operators via `CALL fnx.<algorithm>(...) [YIELD ...]`. Six tasks: w8-projection (authorized projection surface, honest copy boundary); w8-fnx-upstream (borrowed neighbor-cursor/GAT interface); w8-materialization (spillable `MATERIALIZED` path, exposure gate); w8-kernels (masked-semiring SpMV/SpMSpV); w8-witnesses (CGSE flow-through); w8-scheduling (`PrismRegion` bulkhead). Scope is Local single-node analytics over authorized snapshots of any branch/valid-time selection; distributed analytics is out of W8 scope.

## Why (bets, market, goals)
fnx is one of the three closed-universe foundation projects: ~247 KLOC across 12 crates, `fnx-algorithms` alone offering 550+ functions across 25+ families (shortest paths, centrality, communities, flow, matching, isomorphism/VF2++, planarity, spectral, k-core/k-truss, link prediction, DAG ops). The plan's stance (Section 2.2): this is a source catalog and semantics oracle; in-database exposure is staged by projection compatibility, authorization, larger-than-memory execution, and differential gates — not promised on day one. Market: the Neo4j GDS use case without a second engine or an export hop. Bets: B3 — analytics run inside the same execution universe under the same authorization root, not in a sidecar; B5 — fnx's CGSE determinism doctrine (tie-break policies, `ComplexityWitness`, `WitnessLedger`) generalizes from algorithms to query-level plan certificates; B2 — projections ride Strata's tiered adjacency rather than a private CSR copy; B6 — agents receive typed errors (`ResourceExhausted`, `FeatureDisabled`) and inspectable certificates; B1 — any branch or temporal snapshot is analyzable identically under the same visibility rules. Performance goal (Section 17, benchmark-class): LDBC Graphalytics (BFS/PR/WCC/CDLP/LCC/SSSP) within 1.5x of dedicated static analytics engines on transactional storage — the Sortledton bar, beaten.

## Design — normative detail
Five doctrine pillars from Section 11. (1) Surface: only registered, semantically compatible fnx signatures are callable. The versioned `FnxSignatureRegistry` describes per algorithm its graph-input arity, typed parameters/defaults/coercions, output schema, attribute roles (weight, capacity, demand, partition, label, etc.), callback/matcher module type/effects, RNG policy/seed, directed/multigraph/self-loop laws, numeric/determinism profile, complexity witness, and larger-than-memory implementation class; only complete rows are callable, and all input projections and implementation paths ride in the certificate. (2) Honest copy boundary: the current fnx trait borrows `&[usize]`; Strata's compressed `u32/u64` rows cannot safely implement that contract zero-copy, so W8 upstreams a borrowed neighbor-cursor/GAT interface; until then compatibility uses explicit epoch-shared `Vec<usize>` caches labeled `DECODED_CACHE`, never claimed zero-copy; typed directed multigraphs are reduced only through an `AuthorizedProjection` bound by the registered `FnxCallSpec`, and parallel-edge aggregation is never implicit. (3) Witness flow-through: CGSE policy semantics and the `ComplexityWitness` schema are preserved; each in-database witness additionally binds the authorized projection digest, projection-specific n/m, adapter/materialization path, numeric profile, and fnx implementation hash; the ledger folds into the query's plan certificate. (4) Coverage: algorithms not cursor-generic take a `MATERIALIZED` path that streams/spills an authorized projection into a generation-scoped representation; an algorithm becomes a database operator only with a bounded cursor path or a declared external-memory/spill implementation with cleanup and I/O bounds — otherwise it stays in the source catalog rather than violating the larger-than-memory product contract; `ResourceExhausted` is legal only when even the registered minimum resident set or scratch quota is unavailable, never as a substitute for designing the operator. (5) Scheduling: analytics run in dedicated regions on a bulkhead-isolated lane (combinator: `bulkhead`) so a Louvain over 10^9 edges cannot starve p99 OLTP; budgets and cancellation apply; long runs checkpoint progress as obligations; a cancelled community detection cleans up its scratch deterministically.

## Invariants & claim types
FG-INV-20 binds the whole epic: authorization precedes every observation or effect across storage, statistics, routing/scoring, temporal selection, workspace, errors, constraints/witnesses/prepares, derived state, Prism/UDFs, streams, capabilities, replay/export/backup, audit, and observability — Prism is named explicitly; one union-wide authorization decision covers the complete effect set; capability lookup/status/release is uniformly nonrevealing on failure. FG-INV-12: every claimed answer-equivalent spill or materialization preserves logical values, multiplicity, order, visibility, security projection, and AnswerContract. FG-INV-16: no scratch object or obligation is lost, duplicated, or exposed while obligated; every obligation reaches one legal terminal or recoverable state. Claim classes per the constitution: the Graphalytics 1.5x target is benchmark-class; convergence bounds and iteration traces are evidence-class residual artifacts; OLTP isolation under analytics load is SLO/benchmark class, never an invariant.

## Interactions
Consumes: w4-secure-view (sole constructor of `AuthorizedGraphView`/`AuthorizedSnapshot`), w5-executor (spill/morsel machinery), w5-determinism (query-level CGSE), w3-tier-r and w3-vertex-directory (adjacency, ordinal maps), w1-foundation-types. Produces: operators consumed by obs-system-graph (wait-for cycle detection and centrality over the system graph, with the declared `FeatureDisabled` degraded mode); the Prism-vs-standalone-fnx differential corpus for verif-differential (a two-hop oracle chain — fnx is itself NetworkX-parity-locked); batch reference results against which w6-maintainers' delta-PageRank/incremental-CC/k-core maintainers are checked; Graphalytics gates hosted by perf-bench-core.

## Success Criteria
Epic closes when all six tasks are done and: the Prism differential suite (same projected input + same policy vs standalone fnx) is green across all exposed families; Graphalytics baselines are committed within the 1.5x bar with variance-aware gating (the baseline runs execute on §15.6's deterministic apparatus via `perf-bench-core`/`verif-perf-apparatus`, outside this epic's closure — committed-and-green is a gate-g4 requirement; at epic close the bench rows and pinned fixtures must be registered); FG-INV-20 negative matrices cover every Prism entry point; `FeatureDisabled` behavior and its registry row are tested; and an e2e script runs `CALL fnx.pagerank` over a branched, valid-time-sliced graph, cancels one concurrent run mid-flight, and verifies scratch quiescence plus certificate contents — logging projection digest, path label, witness ledger ids, and budget charges at every stage.

## Risks & rejected alternatives
Section 20 risk row: fnx algorithms are not yet trait-generic or external-memory where required — `GraphView` exists with integer rows, but compatible larger-than-memory coverage is partial; this epic's upstream/cursor and materialization work is the mitigation. Rejected: a sidecar analytics engine or export-to-CSR hop (breaks B1/B3 and the single authorization root); zero-copy claims the physical representation cannot honor; raw-graph-vs-filtered-projection differential comparisons; implicit parallel-edge aggregation.

## Provenance
Plan Section 11 (lines 834-857); Section 2.2; Section 12.3; Section 16; Section 17; Sections 18.1-18.2; Section 19 W8 row; Section 20.

title: Deliver the Warden plane: tokens, enforcement, keys, erasure, DP, audit, time authority
description:
## What & scope
Deliver the complete Warden plane (§12) plus its §16 external-authority surface. Warden is not a middleware layer: it is a set of mandatory access types, closed-union durable schemas, and externally anchored evidence chains that every other plane must consume. The epic covers: (1) the threat/authority model instantiated as typed identities and registries; (2) the macaroon capability-token lifecycle with restricted `PolicyIr`, policy/revocation roots, and role-closed `SecurityStateBinding`; (3) mandatory access-type enforcement through the `fgdb-secure-view` facade, hidden-state disclosure contracts, and enforced descriptor masking; (4) derived-state/cache/error authorization via `DerivedIdentity` and `AuthorityReuseLaw`; (5) the encryption/key lifecycle with the two-stage reachability-fenced destruction pipeline (`KeyDestroyProposal` -> `DestroyPending` quarantine -> `KeyDestroyFinalizeSpec` -> `DestroyedPendingCertificate` -> certificate-published `Destroyed`); (6) targeted erasure (`ErasureCutSpec`, `ErasureTombstone` visibility conjunct, `SubjectKeyDomainContract`, `erasure_obligations.toml`); (7) differential privacy with an external irreversible-before-access Renyi debit, protected seed lineage, and Meta-only noise; (8) the two-plane audit architecture — applied vs visible — spanning the external `AuditContinuityRecord` CAS chain, `AuditTicket` gating, the gap-free `AuditVisibilityPipeline`, `AuditExternalResolutionBatch`, the sole release input `AuditVisibilityAdvanceSpec`, and independent protected-output activation; (9) batched activation/disposition with `TimeBoundSubject::ActivationBatch` time evidence; (10) the external time authority from `TimeAuthorityProfile` through `TimeValidationEvidence`, linear `TimeUseGuard`s, and full rotation/retirement; (11) the published authority footprint table, three availability lines, succession protocol, and database-as-isolation-unit doctrine. Children: w9-threat-tokens, w9-enforcement, w9-key-lifecycle, w9-redaction-erasure, w9-dp, w9-dp-continuity-import, w9-audit-continuity, w9-audit-protected-orders, w9-audit-pipeline, w9-audit-release, w9-activation-batching, w9-time-authority, w9-time-rotation, w9-authority-surface.

## Why (bets, market, goals)
B6 (agent-native): mutually hostile agents/tenants share one database, so authorization must be capability-scoped (macaroons with attenuation-only narrowing), branch-aware (the key envelope DAG binds fork epochs — B1), and noninterfering. B5: every security claim is a typed, externally verifiable artifact — signed receipts, threshold-signed continuity records, registered claim classes — never an adjective; leakage bounds are deployment-scoped `StatisticalClaim`s, availability is `slo.toml`, capacity is `FG-CFG`. Market wedge: agent-memory and GraphRAG deployments need provable governance — audit that detects gaps, erasure that provably reaches derived state, DP with an unforgeable budget — offered as first-class ordered commands rather than a proxy bolt-on, without claiming TEE/Byzantine-confidentiality magic.

## Design — normative detail
The trust matrix (§12.1) distinguishes untrusted clients, mutually hostile tenants, honest-but-curious storage, crash-fault replicas, malicious/stale donors, independent transparency witnesses, trusted embedded host code, and a compromised operator/server. The baseline trusts the executing database process and active key boundary; a compromised server can exfiltrate what it can decrypt. Witnessed transparency/audit detect only their scoped history/administrative attacks. Stable identities: `TenantId`, `PrincipalId`, `IssuerId`, `TokenId`, `DatabaseId`, `SecurityPolicyEpoch`, `RevocationIndex`, `DecisionPolicyEpoch`, `KeyEpoch` — distinct wire tags and Rust newtypes, never comparable or substitutable. `EffectiveAuthority` binds tenant/subject/issuer/audience, database security namespace and cluster incarnation, token/security-policy epochs, current revocation index, operation classes, graph/branch/label/edge/property/system-field/temporal scopes, procedure/UDF/module ObjectIds and invocation mode, external-I/O classes, replay evidence/resolver closure, redaction profile, and resource ceiling. Operation classes are exactly `Read, Mutate, Ddl, Subscribe, Analytics, Replay, ExecuteProcedure, InstallModule, ExternalIo, Export, Backup, Restore, Observe, Admin, KeyManage, Replicate`. The architectural spine of the plane is the two-plane audit split: Semantic applied state may advance ahead of publicly visible state only through the rooted gap-free audit visibility pipeline, and only the Protocol-plane `AuditVisibilityAdvanceSpec` moves the visible endpoint; delivery activation is a third, time-authority-gated step deliberately kept off the audit prefix.

## Invariants & claim types
FG-INV-20 binds the whole epic: authorization precedes every observation or effect across storage, statistics, routing/scoring, temporal selection, workspace, errors, constraints/witnesses/prepares, derived state, Prism/UDFs, streams, capabilities, replay/export/backup, audit, and observability; every authority-bearing durable schema binds one complete `SecurityStateBinding` (or exact certified shard projection); a protected candidate becomes observable only after its signer-locked terminal event, external resolution batch, and gap-free visibility advance. FG-INV-16: no privacy charge/seed/result, audit freeze/plan/lock/share/pipeline entry, or obligation is lost, duplicated, refunded, or exposed while obligated. FG-INV-04's applied-vs-visible clause and erasure conjunct, FG-INV-13's envelope/destruction clauses, and FG-INV-19's `Redacted` replay arm bind children. Claim classes: mutual-information/channel-capacity results are `StatisticalClaim`s; availability lines and per-tenant ticket SLOs are `slo.toml`; maintenance-stream capacity is FG-CFG-04; required-audit throughput is a benchmark-class governance profile.

## Interactions
Consumes w1-authz-policy (nonconstructible permits, restricted verifier IR), w1-crypto (profiles, constant-time, external audit gate), w2-root-bootstrap (RootManifest/RootSlot D2 publication), w2-commit-protocol (§5.2 steps that independently verify permits and carry terminal gates). Produces the authorization boundary consumed by w4-secure-view/w4-coordinator, the audit visibility machinery consumed by w10-result-machines/w10-capabilities, the time evidence consumed by every lease/capability owner, and the authority surface consumed by obs-slo and risk-register.

## Success Criteria
Epic closes when all fourteen children close and three cross-cutting e2e flows pass with full structured logging: (1) a Required-profile mutation round-trips ticket issuance CAS -> admission -> claim -> event/resolution -> external batch -> visibility advance -> batched activation -> guarded output, with every boundary crash-injected; (2) an `ErasureCutSpec` installed on a subject-keyed domain reaches every registered derived surface and downgrades replay attributably; (3) a DP charge survives lost external replies and a backup-behind restore without a double debit. Detailed-logging bar for all three flows: every boundary emits a structured event carrying at minimum {flow_id, step_name, role_and_group, ticket/pipeline_order or charge_operation_id, relevant head digests and cas_versions before/after, verdict, retry-idempotency marker}, with secrets appearing only as commitments, so each chain can be reconstructed and verified from logs alone after the run; a flow whose log chain has a gap fails the epic gate. Noninterference differential suites (hidden-vs-removed) and the governance bench profile (§12.8) are release gates.

## Risks & rejected alternatives
Rejected: TEE/FHE/MPC/ORAM in the v1 threat model (§3.4 item i) — the plan states honestly that a compromised process exfiltrates what it can decrypt; universal noninterference or global bits/query ceilings (only deployment-specific `StatisticalClaim`s); per-tenant intra-database audit visibility (registered rejection — cumulative candidate roots demand one total admission order); unaudited in-house cryptography (release-blocking external audit required). Risks: external-authority availability sits on the visibility path (mitigated by the three-line availability doctrine and backpressure); schema breadth of the audit plane (mitigated by registry generation and bijection CI).

title: UBS misclassifies non-secret sketch-state digest equality as a secret comparison
description: UBS v5.3.7 exits 1 on crates/fgdb-reference/src/lib.rs:873 at commit 5c9088d, on the comparison actual != before_state_digest. Both operands are non-secret canonical sketch-state digests used to validate an ordinary before-image and form a typed SketchBeforeMismatch; they are not credentials, HMACs, signatures, bearer tokens, CSRF values, or any other timing-sensitive secret. The finding predates fgdb-reference-si-edge-delete-constraint-lmtc (git blame 08bfadf0), but scanning the three changed files cannot produce the mandated exit-0 result because UBS scans whole files. A pinned git-archive HEAD scan and the live scan each report the same sole critical class and site. Do not contort this equality into constant-time code and do not add a broad ignore merely to manufacture green. Acceptance: narrow rust_constant_time_compare_matches upstream or provide a checked, line-specific false-positive disposition that keeps new or uncertain secret-comparison findings fail-closed, then demonstrate attributable UBS exit 0 on this file.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
THE HEADLINE IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE HYPOTHESIS, AND IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE TIME SAVING. The catalog lane and the crate lane are NOT independent. A registries-only increment CAN break crates/**, and it breaks it at COMPILE time, not as a test failure. So the lane discipline rests on a premise that is false in one specific, narrow, demonstrable way. The time-saving question is real but strictly secondary, and the scoping rule cannot be "registries-only increments skip crates".

=== THE COUPLING, PROVEN IN BOTH DIRECTIONS ===
crates/fgdb-types/src/refs.rs:29 compiles the generated projection into the crate:
    const LOGICAL_OBJECT_KIND_REGISTRY: &[u8] = include_bytes!("../../../registries/logical_object_kinds.toml");
and then asserts against it at compile time, in two ways:
 (a) PER KIND, for each of the 10 declared codes, that the registry contains the exact byte run
     `object_kind = 0xNNNN\nname = "Name"\nstatus = "active"` — so a change to any active row's code, name OR status breaks the build;
 (b) BY COUNT, `count_bytes(REGISTRY, b"status = \"active\"") == LogicalObjectKindCode::ALL_ACTIVE.len()` — so adding ANY new active row breaks the build even if no existing row is touched.
DEMONSTRATED, not inferred. Adding one `status = "active"` row to a scratch copy of the projection and compiling the refs module gives
    error[E0080]: evaluation panicked: assertion failed: count_bytes(LOGICAL_OBJECT_KIND_REGISTRY, ACTIVE_STATUS_ROW) == ...
    evaluation of `refs::_` failed here
and the identical probe against the pristine projection compiles clean. So the failure is real, it is a hard compile error, and it is attributable to the registry file alone.
BLAST RADIUS: 7 of 10 crates depend on fgdb-types (fgdb-types, fgdb-codec, fgdb-delta-types, fgdb-evidence, fgdb-resource, fgdb-sketch, fgdb-calibrate). A catalog increment that activates a logical kind therefore fails the build of seven crates, which is exactly what the full-workspace cargo test is there to catch.
This is BY DESIGN, not a bug — it is the structural registry binding landed in 6b987b3, replacing a doc comment that admitted the binding was NOT compile-time enforced. It is good engineering. It simply also means the lanes are coupled.

=== EVERY OTHER COUPLING PATH IS CLEAN, AUDITED EXHAUSTIVELY ===
  include_str!/include_bytes! in crates/**      : exactly ONE, the line above (sweep positive-controlled against tools/, which does use them)
  build.rs under crates/**                      : 0
  crates/*/Cargo.toml depending on registry-check: 0
  env!/option_env! in crates/**                  : 0
  path literals naming registries/ or the g0 scripts: only DOC COMMENTS in fgdb-claim (prose cross-references, no compile-time read)
So the reach-in is a single file and a single registry. NOTHING in crates/** reads registries/appendix_a_catalog.toml, durable_fields.toml, wire_types.toml, physical_record_kinds.toml, bootstrap_frames.toml, prebootstrap_artifact_kinds.toml, architecture_decisions.toml, tools/registry-check/**, or either g0 script.

=== THE PRECISE, CONDITIONAL RULE ===
A catalog increment can affect crates/** IF AND ONLY IF it changes registries/logical_object_kinds.toml such that either an active row's (object_kind, name, status) triple moves, or the total count of `status = "active"` lines changes. Otherwise the coupling is provably absent.
Consequence worth noting for the swarm: minting a RESERVED logical kind does NOT trip it, because both assertions key on `status = "active"`. That is why a04's ConfigurationState mint and a15's KeyDestroyProposal mint did not break any crate — and why nobody has noticed the coupling. It will bite the first increment that ACTIVATES a kind, and it will present as an unrelated-looking compile error in seven crates.

=== THE MEASURED COST, WHICH IS THE SECONDARY FINDING ===
  scoped `cargo test -p registry-check`, warm: 28.6s for 8 test binaries
  full-workspace `cargo test` in the composite gate: the dominant term; the current holder's run is remote clippy 14m15s plus a full test it expects at ~25m, i.e. roughly 40 minutes per catalog increment, serialized behind one token.
My own cheap-path measurements bound the rest precisely and none of it explains the 40 minutes: architecture-check 0.63s prebuilt vs 9.1s warm cargo; identity suite 29.2s vs 32.6s where execution dominates so no build trick helps.

=== WHAT I AM NOT PROPOSING ===
I am NOT proposing to skip cargo test and I have NOT touched scripts/check.sh. AGENTS.md makes `cargo test` a hard exit-zero gate before any handoff, and the coupling above means a blanket scoped gate for this lane would be UNSOUND for the activate-a-kind case. The doctrine question — whether a catalog increment that provably does not alter logical_object_kinds.toml active rows may run a scoped gate, and how that predicate would be enforced rather than trusted — belongs to the owner, exactly as with fgdb-u3gr.
If it is ever taken up, the predicate must be MECHANICAL, not a judgement: something like "if git diff --name-only touches registries/logical_object_kinds.toml, run the full workspace; otherwise scoped" — and note the honest weakness of that specific form, which is that it trusts the diff rather than the assertion, so a regenerated-but-identical file would be treated as a change (safe) while a hand-edited crate macro list would be missed (unsafe, but that is a crate-lane edit and would run the full gate anyway).

comments.text:
THE PIN SPLIT IS STOOD DOWN BY THE OWNER, AND THE EVIDENCE SUPPORTS THAT RATHER THAN MERELY PERMITTING IT. Recording the full analysis here so whoever picks it up post-freeze does not re-derive it. NOTE I AM DELIBERATELY NOT CREATING A BEAD FOR IT RIGHT NOW: bead creation moves the provenance pins and therefore needs the catalog token for the same-commit re-freeze, I have just released catalog, and I already paid that exact out-of-order cost once today. It wants a bead created INSIDE a future catalog hold.

WHAT THE SPLIT WAS FOR: filing any bead moves three provenance pins in tools/registry-check/src/architecture.rs, the file every Appendix A increment edits, so bead creation serialized against all catalog work.

WHY THE ORIGINAL DESIGN DID NOT WORK (Finding B). Moving the consts alone does not decouple anything. Filing a bead touches FOUR things, and only one is the proposed new file:
  1. .beads/issues.jsonl                                     -> beads token
  2. registries/architecture_decisions.toml [bead_provenance] -> CATALOG token
  3. the count/hash consts                                    -> would move to the new file
  4. PINNED_SEMANTIC_CONTRACT_HASH                             -> CATALOG token
(4) is unavoidable because recompute_semantic_contract_hash reads registry.bead_provenance — via a LOCAL ALIAS `let policy = &registry.bead_provenance;`, which is why a token-grep for the field name came back empty while the empirical evidence said otherwise. The evidence was right. So after the original split, (2) and (4) still require catalog and the serialization is unchanged.

THE AMENDED 3-PART DESIGN THAT WOULD WORK, and its true size:
  (i)   move the 12-const cluster (not 3 — all four resolution-class counts are live and movable) to src/bead_provenance.rs, pub use re-exported. Small, self-contained, and by itself COSMETIC since it does not decouple.
  (ii)  move [bead_provenance] plus the [[bead_family]] and [[bead_override]] tables into registries/bead_provenance.toml. This is NOT a file move: those blocks are parsed inside architecture_decisions.toml's single closed-key validator, so it needs a second parse entry point, a split allowed-key list, a split require_present list, six hardcoded "architecture_decisions.toml.*" error contexts rewritten, a [registry] header and epoch for the new file, the e2e path at g0_architecture_decisions_e2e.sh:124, and its staging fixtures.
  (iii) remove those three from recompute_semantic_contract_hash and add PINNED_BEAD_PROVENANCE_CONTRACT_HASH. Without (iii), (ii) buys nothing — the hash still moves.
So it is a loader restructuring plus a new registry file plus a contract-hash split, during a G0 freeze, on the most load-bearing pin machinery in the repo. Larger than one increment.

THE COVERAGE PROOF IS ALREADY DISCHARGED, so this part need not be redone. recompute_semantic_contract_hash appends 50 tagged fields in FIVE disjoint prefix groups that are CONTIGUOUS in transcript order: decision.* 23 (positions 1-23), profile.* 10 (24-33), bead_provenance.* 9 (34-42), bead_family.* 5 (43-47), bead_override.* 3 (48-50). uniq -c over the tag prefixes yields exactly five runs, so there is no interleaving and the split is a clean prefix/suffix cut at 33/34. Retained hash keeps 1-33; the new hash takes 34-50. Union 33 + 17 = 50 = the current total; intersection empty. Three structural facts make it safe rather than merely arithmetic: there is NO untagged head or terminator (the fn is `let mut transcript = Vec::new()` ... `format!("fnv1a64:{...}", fnv1a64(&transcript))`), so nothing must be duplicated into both successors; the cut being prefix/suffix means relative order within each successor is unchanged; and each group's sort key lives inside its own group. Expect BOTH pin values to change, since each hashes a shorter transcript — derive from checker output.

THE HONEST COST, which is why standing it down is right. Bead creation collided with catalog work exactly ONCE today — my own out-of-order br create — and the total cost was one extra commit by cod_2 plus about five minutes. The forty-minute catalog increments were caused by full-workspace gate runs and long increments, not by bead-pin contention. So the split does not fix what it was sold as fixing. See this bead's own finding for the gate-time analysis, which is the larger term.

RECOMMENDATION FOR THE EVENTUAL OWNER: do (i)+(ii)+(iii) together or not at all, after the freeze, as its own multi-commit piece of work with the coverage proof above re-verified against the then-current transcript. Do not land (i) alone; it changes nothing and adds a module for no benefit.

title: Replace product PassThroughValidator with first-committer-wins on live WriteBatch
description:
G1 slice of Gap 2 (docs/REALITY_CHECK_AND_BRIDGE_PLAN.md): replace the product-path PassThroughValidator instance for the live WriteBatch family with first-committer-wins against the batch's basis snapshot. This is NOT Graph-SSI, NOT the merge ladder, NOT WriteCoordinator, NOT session/txn ownership.

## Why this is a capability, not ceremony

Today `CommitCoordinator::open` installs `PassThroughValidator` (`crates/fgdb-chronicle/src/commit.rs`) and the product `Database` write path never replaces it. Sequential `WriteBatch` updates of the same vertex both commit: the live fold catches create/create (`AlreadyLive`) but not update/update lost-writes. Gate G1's Genesis slice requires "commit validation is not PassThroughValidator."

## Architecture (do not invert)

- Chronicle owns the SEAM: `CommitValidator` + `PassThroughValidator` fixture + `set_validator`. Keep PassThrough; crash-point tests still use it. Do not make Chronicle default to graph-aware validation (layering: no LogicalDeltaTemplate in chronicle).
- Product `fgdb::Database` owns the INSTANCE: a `FirstCommitterWinsValidator` implementing `CommitValidator`, installed on every product open (`open` / `open_with_vfs` / bind). Decode `draft.capsule_plaintext` as `LogicalDeltaTemplate` (those bytes are `prepare_capsule`'s canonical template). Conflict keys are `touched_elements` (`crates/fgdb/src/lib.rs`).
- Validator is a function of (draft, explicitly constructed state). `validate` still takes no `Cx`.
- A rejection is `CommitError::Rejected`: no durable capsule, no marker, sequence not consumed, coordinator not poisoned.

## Required behavior

First-committer-wins: a WriteBatch prepared against snapshot seq B is rejected if any ElementId in its write-set was mutated by a commit with seq > B. Disjoint write-sets against the same basis both commit.

Because the coordinator is still single-writer, "two concurrent writers" is: two prepares against the same live snapshot, then two commits. First overlapping commit wins; second aborts with a typed `WriteError` arm (not a generic `WriteError::Commit` wrap). Sequential `write()` against the already-advanced snapshot must keep working (basis is current ⇒ no false abort).

## Implementation plan (owned files)

1. `crates/fgdb/src/fcw.rs` (new module — new functionality, not a V2 of an existing file): `FirstCommitterWinsValidator` { last_writer: BTreeMap<ElementId, CommitSeq> }. On Ok, record this draft's keys at `draft.commit_seq`. On overlap with last_writer[key] > basis, reject with `law = "FG-LAW-FCW-01"` (do NOT bump `expected_enforced_invariants`; this is not an FG-INV promotion).
2. `crates/fgdb/src/lib.rs`: `mod fcw`; install the validator on product open; map `CommitError::Rejected` with that law to a distinct `WriteError` arm; add `prepare_write` + `commit_prepared` (or equivalent) so two templates can share a basis. Do not change the existing `write()` sequential path's snapshot fold.
3. Chronicle tests: rejection still leaves no durable residue (seq free). PassThrough remains the default on a bare coordinator.
4. Product test: overlapping vertex property updates, two prepares, first commits, second aborts, reopen matches only the first; disjoint updates both commit.

## Acceptance (orchestrator closes; agents do not)

Positive:
- Product open path: `Database` coordinator validator is NOT `PassThroughValidator` (Debug identity / type name).
- Two prepared overlapping WriteBatches against one snapshot: first `commit_prepared` returns Ok; second returns the typed FCW abort; `commit_seq` of the second did not land; reopen + `fgdb-reference` replay agree with the first write only.
- Two prepared disjoint WriteBatches against one snapshot: both commit.

Planted negative (must fail if someone cheats):
- A test that installs PassThrough on a Database and expects the overlapping second write to abort MUST fail (proves FCW is the thing doing the abort, not the fold).
- Deleting `FirstCommitterWinsValidator::validate`'s overlap check must turn the product overlapping test red.

No-claim boundary: not SSI, not rw-cycles, not merge-ladder rebase, not multi-process writers, not promoting FG-INV-*. PassThrough stays as the chronicle fixture.

## Code-first wave

`cargo check -p CRATE` only. No `cargo test`, no `scripts/check.sh`, no rch exec. Commit immediately. Do not `br close`. Orchestrator batch-verifies and closes.

title: All 20 FG-INV clauses are stub: zero live checkers, so 'CI cross-checks every ID has a live checker' passes over an empty set
description:
## The measurement (0ada651, with a control)

    invariants: 20   clauses: 20
    entrypoint resolutions (checker + negative_test): live=0  stub=40  unresolved=0
    FG-INV ids with EVERY entrypoint live: 0
    clause status histogram: {"stub": 20}

CONTROL: the probe asserts `claims_hash_twenty_id_pin` resolves among the 78 checker_index rows
before any zero is reported. It does. So `live=0` is a fact about the registry, not a broken
lookup. Reproduce with `model::load_registries` + a fold over `invariants.invariants[].clauses`;
do not grep.

## Why it is a bug and not just "pre-Genesis"

Stub registration before Genesis is explicitly allowed by checker_index.toml's own header, and
nothing here says the twenty should already be enforced. The defect is that **nothing reports the
emptiness.** AGENTS.md, Spec-First Workflow item 2: "CI cross-checks that every ID has a live
checker." With zero live checkers that cross-check quantifies over an empty set and passes — the
strongest possible form of a vacuous gate, and indistinguishable at the exit code from a spine
that is fully enforced.

The hard rule directly below it — "no subsystem ships against an unenforced invariant. A
workstream exit gate (G1-G4) cannot pass while any invariant it depends on lacks a live checker"
— is therefore currently unenforceable in the direction that matters: every G1 gate would have to
fail, and nothing computes that.

## The law that should exist

Not "make the twenty live" — that is the whole verification programme, not a bead. The law is
that the emptiness must be VISIBLE and must have a declared expectation, in the shape
`Manifest::expected_reachable_clauses` already uses in this very repo:

    declare, in invariants.toml, the number of clauses expected to be live at the current gate
    (0 pre-Genesis), and fail when the measured count differs in EITHER direction.

Both directions matter. Too few = a clause silently regressed to stub. Too many = a clause was
promoted to live without the gate review the doctrine requires
(cf. fgdb-clause-promotion-to-live-is-unguarded-nllh, which is the promotion half of this).

## Relationship to the neighbours, so nobody re-derives it

- `fgdb-validator-laws-never-witnessed-firing-xnxy` — 253/404 violation codes never asserted.
  Same question ("which declared law was ever observed to reject something") one level down, at
  the code rather than the clause. One instrument should answer both; commented there.
- `fgdb-checker-index-live-is-only-file-existence-tl0o` — what `live` PROVES. This bead is about
  what happens when the live set is EMPTY, which tl0o's fix does not address.

title: Negative fixture searches for a literal released epoch (registry_epoch = 1); it stops matching when two registries bump
description:
Found by re-deriving fgdb-glo0's premise at HEAD 4fcc68a. glo0's filed defect is DEAD
(fixed by 47df9c4 under fgdb-un4g) and its deferred sweep came back CLEAN — with this
one residual, which is a DIFFERENT failure mode from the one glo0 filed.

## THE COUPLING
`tools/registry-check/tests/identity.rs:615-616` builds a negative fixture by
    source.replacen("registry_epoch = 1\n",
                    "registry_epoch = 1\nunknown_projection_epoch_key = true\n", 1)
The search string is a LITERAL RELEASED EPOCH VALUE. It matches today only because two
projection epochs in `registries/appendix_a_catalog.toml` still sit at 1:
    physical_record_kinds       registry_epoch = 1   <- first occurrence, the one hit
    prebootstrap_artifact_kinds registry_epoch = 1
Every other projection epoch has moved (logical_object_kinds 62, wire_types 42,
durable_fields 77, bootstrap_frames 2).

## TRIGGER
When BOTH of those registries bump past 1, `replacen` matches nothing, the "mutated"
source equals the original, `parse_catalog` returns Ok, and the harness's
`.expect_err("unknown projection epoch key must fail closed")` PANICS.

## SEVERITY: LOW, and measured rather than assumed
It FAILS LOUD, not vacuously. I read the harness rather than guessing: the consumer is
`.expect_err(...)` followed by `has_violation(...)`, so a lost mutation panics with a
message naming the test. It does NOT silently pass. That is the opposite of glo0's filed
defect, which surfaced as twelve unrelated-looking ordinary-union failures.
This is filed so the panic is self-explaining when it arrives, not because it is urgent.

## FIX, same shape as the one that closed glo0
Do not hardcode a released epoch as a search string. Either target the projection block
by its registry NAME (`registry = "physical_record_kinds"`) and inject after it, or
interpolate the epoch from the loaded catalog the way `ordinary_top_level_union_fixture`
now does with its `@EPOCH@` placeholder — a placeholder that is not valid TOML, so a
substitution that stops happening is a loud parse error rather than a silent no-op.

## CONTROL for whoever fixes it
Mutate a scratch copy of the catalog so NO projection epoch equals 1, then run the test.
PRE-FIX it must PANIC on `.expect_err`; POST-FIX it must still find its violation. A fix
that makes the test pass in both states has made the fixture vacuous and is wrong.

## VERIFICATION LOOP — lock-free, no cargo, no build slot
  CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR=<repo>/tools/registry-check rustc --edition 2024 \
    --crate-type rlib --crate-name registry_check tools/registry-check/src/lib.rs -o <sp>/l.rlib
  CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR=<repo>/tools/registry-check rustc --edition 2024 --test \
    --crate-name identity tools/registry-check/tests/identity.rs \
    --extern registry_check=<sp>/l.rlib -L <sp> -o <sp>/t
Build INSIDE a dir carrying rust-toolchain.toml or the rlib and test disagree (E0514).

title: validate_script_closure does not recurse: scripts/lib/*.sh is claimed by no gate row, including gate_verdict.sh
description:
MEASURED at c8c8781, reading tools/registry-check/src/validate.rs:1045. validate_script_closure builds its on-disk set with fs::read_dir(root/"scripts") filtered to names ending .sh. read_dir is NOT recursive, so the set contains only DIRECT CHILDREN of scripts/. Everything under scripts/lib/ and scripts/git_hooks/ is invisible to it.

WHY THAT MATTERS. The [[script_disposition]] mechanism exists (fgdb-orphan-w1-e2e-gates-unregistered-unrun-vuq8) because a shell deliverable could sit in scripts/ carrying every signal of a gate while no runner and no registry knew it existed; six did. That closure is enforced one directory deep. One level down it does not exist at all, so a .sh in scripts/lib/ can be a gate nobody runs, or dead code, and nothing in the repository states which.

THE FILE THIS EXEMPTS IS THE MOST LOAD-BEARING SHELL FILE IN THE REPO.
scripts/lib/gate_verdict.sh defines the verdict contract every one of the 11 gates reports under, plus the fgdb-49ng tree-stability tripwire. It is claimed by NO [[checker]] row and NO [[script_disposition]] row. Same for scripts/lib/private_subject.sh.

WHAT IS AND IS NOT COVERED TODAY, so this is not overstated:
 * COVERED: check.sh file-coverage closure claims it via the *.sh|*.bash arm of coverage_of(), so it does get bash -n + shellcheck.
 * COVERED: its CONTRACT conformance is checked indirectly — verdict_contract_violations requires every enumerated gate to source it.
 * NOT COVERED: the row -> file and file -> row closure. Nothing declares what scripts/lib/gate_verdict.sh IS. A new file dropped beside it inherits the same silence.

DISCLOSURE: the three files landed by fgdb-eesn at c8c8781 (scripts/lib/landing_lease.sh, scripts/git_hooks/pre-commit.sh, scripts/git_hooks/install.sh) sit in exactly this blind spot and therefore owed no registry row and needed no catalog token. The placement is the established convention rather than an evasion — gate_verdict.sh and private_subject.sh were already there, and libraries do not belong in the gate namespace — but the exemption is real and was noticed while using it, so it is reported rather than left for someone else to find.

LIKELY REPAIR: recurse, and add a role to [[script_disposition]] for a library (something like role = "library", meaning sourced by gates, runs no assertions of its own, registered as an artifact of the gates that source it). Beware the obvious wrong fix: registering a library as a [[checker]] would make check.sh EXECUTE it, and gate_verdict.sh registers no gate and asserts nothing, so it would report UNRUN on every run — a guard disabled by its own trigger.

CONTROL THE FIX. Whatever lands must fail when a new unclaimed .sh appears under scripts/lib/, proven by adding one and watching it red. A closure that passes proves nothing until it can fail; the enumeration-vs-glob lesson from fgdb-mt2b applies verbatim here.

title: g0_identity_e2e write-through guard hashes .git, so it false-reds under any concurrent pane
description:
scripts/g0_identity_e2e.sh's final assertion compares snapshot_nonprojection_tree($ROOT) before and after the evidence gate and dies with 'source root changed during evidence gate (write-through guard fired)'. That function runs 'find .' from the repo ROOT and excludes only the six generated projection TOMLs -- there is NO .git exclusion. It therefore hashes .git/index, .git/logs/HEAD, refs and objects, all of which move whenever ANY other pane commits, and the guard fires for a reason that has nothing to do with the change under test.

MEASURED, both directions:
  live repo, my worktree:   91 passed, 1 failed, exit 1 -- the ONLY failure is the guard
  quiet root, same content: 92 passed, 0 failed, exit 0 -- ALL GREEN
The quiet root was the identical worktree copied via 'git ls-files | tar' into a
directory with no .git and no other writers. 91+1 vs 92+0 differ by exactly that one
assertion, which is what identifies it as the guard rather than a content difference.

It fired on two consecutive live runs about 20 minutes apart while 8 panes were
committing, so in this swarm it is closer to always-red than intermittently-red.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND NOISE: it is the LAST assertion before the verdict, so it
converts a fully green 91-assertion run into exit 1. An agent that reads only the
exit code concludes its own change broke the gate, and an agent that learns to
ignore the gate loses all 91 real assertions.

FIX: exclude ./.git from both find invocations in snapshot_nonprojection_tree. The
guard's real purpose -- proving the gate never writes through to the source tree --
is fully served by the tracked files, and .git is not something the checker writes.
A control that must still fire after the fix: touch a tracked non-projection file
mid-gate and confirm the guard still dies.
